tagline.text: An emerald crater lake where lunch is served on a bamboo raft

children.text: Considered the cleanest of San Pablo's seven lakes in Laguna, this crater lake lets you drift slowly across forest-ringed green water on a bamboo raft (balsa) while enjoying a lunch prepared by local residents. It's a peaceful lake that makes for an easy day trip from Manila.
Lake Pandin lies in San Pablo City, Laguna, about

southeast of Manila. San Pablo is known as the "City of Seven Lakes" for the seven volcanic lakes scattered in and around it — Sampaloc, Palakpakin, Calibato, Mohicap, Bunot, Yambo, and Pandin — and Pandin is considered the most pristine of them, with clear water and forest that has stayed largely intact. It's about
15–20 minutes
by car from downtown, heading northeast toward San Lorenzo village.

The seven lakes are shallow "maars," craters formed when underground magma met groundwater and exploded in the volcanic zone between Mount Makiling and Mount Banahaw. Lake Pandin is a small, roughly circular lake covering about
20.5 hectares
, reaching a maximum depth of around
; coconut palms and tropical trees cover its steep crater walls, giving the water a deep emerald color. Right next to it, separated by a narrow strip of land, lies its twin, Lake Yambo (about
28.5 hectares

A legend surrounds the two lakes. A young man named Yambo fell in love with a woman named Pandin, who was cursed so that disaster would strike if her feet ever touched the ground. Unaware of the curse, he set her down on the earth — the ground split open, heavy rain poured down, and the two lakes were formed. To this day, the pair are spoken of side by side, like a couple in love.

The heart of a Pandin trip is the bamboo raft tour run by lakeside residents. You board a wide, roofed raft that's pulled slowly across the lake by hand on a rope, eat a simple country lunch on board — grilled tilapia, paco (fern) salad, and the like — and then swim in the middle of the lake wearing a life vest. There are no rides or facilities, but it suits families, groups of friends, and weekend travelers who want a quiet escape from city noise.
A resident cooperative runs rafts that circle the lake over about
2 hours
. With no engine — just a rope being pulled — the raft moves so quietly that all you hear is water and birdsong.

Grilled tilapia, paco salad, shrimp fritters called okoy, a pork dish, rice, and fruit are laid out on a banana leaf. This country-style spread eaten in the middle of the lake is the highlight of a Pandin trip.
You can jump from the raft into the clear lake while wearing a life vest. The water runs deep and cool, so wear a life vest even if you're a confident swimmer.
Walk out onto the narrow strip of land separating Pandin and Yambo to see both lakes in turn. Yambo is wider and more open, with views of the mountain range toward Mount Banahaw.
It's about
15–20 minutes
on foot along a dirt path through coconut groves and forest, from the roadside entrance down to the lake. Early morning brings birdsong and a lake still veiled in mist.

1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
and look down on Lakes Yambo and Palakpakin, plus Mount San Cristobal and Mount Banahaw.

blocks.title: Lake Sampaloc and Downtown San Pablo

children.text: Lake Sampaloc, the largest of the seven, sits behind city hall and has a walking path around it plus lakeside restaurants — a good afternoon stop after the Pandin tour. Visit nearby San Pablo Cathedral while you're there.

If you're staying overnight, try to arrive at Pandin by
6–7am
. The lake is most beautiful before the mist clears, and it's much quieter before group tours arrive.

Take a Lucena (Quezon)-bound bus from the Buendia (Gil Puyat), Cubao, or Alabang terminal in Pasay/Manila and get off at San Pablo. Operators like JAC Liner, DLTB, and Lucena Lines run frequently; the trip takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours 30 minutes
, with one-way fares around
Tell the conductor "San Pablo" and they'll drop you near SM San Pablo or a downtown stop. Buses back to Manila get crowded on weekend afternoons, so leave yourself extra time on the return trip.
From downtown San Pablo (near the cathedral), take a jeepney bound for Nagcarlan, Liliw, or Rizal and ask to be dropped at the Lake Pandin entrance. It takes about
15–20 minutes
, for around
Chartering a tricycle (a "special trip") costs about
one-way. Return rides can be scarce, so it's easier to agree on a waiting time and round-trip fare with the driver up front.
From the roadside entrance down to the lake is about a
15–20 minute
walk along a dirt path through coconut groves. It gets slippery after rain, so closed shoes are better than sandals.
From Manila, take the SLEX to the Santo Tomas exit, then follow the Maharlika Highway (AH26) to San Pablo. It takes about
2–3 hours
depending on traffic; from downtown, head toward San Lorenzo and park at a private lot near the entrance (about
Southern Laguna's dry season runs
December–May
December–February
in particular has cool mornings and evenings and little rain, keeping the dirt path dry and the lake at its clearest.
March–May
brings midday temperatures up to
, but since the lake is shaded by surrounding forest and the water stays cool, it's actually a great time to swim.
June–November
is the rainy season, with frequent afternoon showers, and
July–October

can see typhoons crossing southern Luzon. Rain turns the dirt path to the lake muddy and can suspend the raft tour, so check the weather and whether it's operating before you set out. The best time of day is

, when the water is calm and the light is soft; weekends, holidays, and Holy Week draw group tours, so a weekday visit is recommended. San Pablo City often holds a coconut festival timed to its patron saint's feast day in
January
most years, so check the city's tourism office for the schedule.

There's no lodging right at Lake Pandin, so most visitors come as a day trip; if you're staying over, downtown San Pablo is the most convenient. Downtown has business hotels and B&Bs at about
a night, and near Lake Sampaloc there are cozy lodgings converted from old mansions. For a more relaxed stay, you could also stay at Villa Escudero Resort, about
30–45 minutes
by car, and combine both spots.

Lunch at Pandin is cooked by lakeside residents themselves and brought out to the raft. The standard spread includes grilled tilapia raised in the lake, paco (fern) salad with tomato and egg, shrimp fritters called okoy, grilled pork liempo, rice, and seasonal fruit, with fresh coconut (buko) available to order separately. The menu and headcount are usually settled when you book.

San Pablo is known for coconut farming, so Laguna specialties like buko pie, espasol (a cylindrical rice-flour sweet), and the coconut spirit lambanog are easy to find. Along Lake Sampaloc in front of city hall, a cluster of restaurants offers lake-view dining — a good stop for coffee and a snack after the tour.

Rafts book up early on weekends and holidays, so contact the cooperative in advance, via Facebook or similar, to set your date, group size, and lunch menu. Walk-in registration is usually fine on weekdays.
Raft tour pricing is often based on a minimum group size, usually around 4 people. If there are only two of you, the per-person rate may go up, so check in advance.
It's convenient to wear your swimsuit under your clothes. Changing rooms and restrooms are basic, so bring a towel, a change of clothes, and a plastic bag.
There's no ATM at the entrance or lakeside, and card payment isn't accepted. Bring enough cash for the tour and transportation.
The raft has a roof, but sunlight reflecting off the water is still strong. Bring sunscreen and a hat, and keep your phone in a waterproof pouch.
Arriving at
7–9am
lets you catch the mist and still water, and it's a good time for photos before group tours arrive.
On your way back, combining Lake Sampaloc, San Pablo Cathedral, and a buko pie shop makes for a full half-day itinerary.
Climbing Mount Mabilog requires a local guide, and an early-morning climb before the Pandin tour works well.
The lake reaches about
at its deepest and the water runs cool. Wear a life vest even if you're a confident swimmer, and keep children under close supervision.
Standing up or crowding to one side of the raft can tip it. Follow the operator's instructions on how to spread out your seating.
The dirt path from the entrance to the lake turns to slippery mud after rain. Wear non-slip shoes during the rainy season.
Don't throw food waste or plastic into the lake. It's a livelihood source for local residents, and San Pablo's seven lakes have ongoing conservation efforts to address water pollution.
The tour may be suspended during thunder, lightning, or heavy rain. If there's a typhoon advisory, postpone your visit and check the latest notices.
Mosquitoes and insects are fairly common, so bring insect repellent.
